title: What We Lost When We Lost Home Ec
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of home economics ("homec") from 19th-century farm household labor and the rise of literacy, cooking schools, and the 1862 Morrill Act, through its founding as a college field, the Lake Placid Conferences and naming of the field, the USDA Bureau of Home Economics and its work on the poverty line, school lunches, and food-company recipes, to its school-level heyday with egg and flour "babies," its decline after standardized testing, No Child Left Behind, and feminist critiques, its rebrand as Family and Consumer Sciences, and modern concerns about basic life skills, financial literacy, and chores. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about a Rockettes select episode.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about their aprons, construction noise next door, and fire trucks during past recordings.

segments.title: Hosts' home ec class memories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck recall taking home ec in high school, note boys were a minority in the class, and that home ec classrooms were disappearing from schools.

segments.title: Home ec defined and early farm life
segments.summary: The hosts define home economics as a class teaching life skills and describe the grueling household work of 19th-century farm women before it existed.

segments.title: Feminism and the push-pull over home ec
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss the debate over whether home ec reinforced women's confinement or opened science careers for women.

segments.title: Origins: literacy, cooking schools, Morrill Act, industrialization
segments.summary: Literacy spread, cookbooks and domestic guides proliferated, cooking schools emerged, the 1862 Morrill Act created land grant colleges open to women, and industrialization left women without intergenerational knowledge, creating demand for home ec.

segments.title: Ellen Swallow Richards
segments.summary: Ellen Swallow Richards is described as the most important early figure in home economics: a chemist, the first woman to get an MIT degree, and the first woman MIT instructor, who ran a sanitary chemistry lab doing water and air quality work; home ec served as a back door for women into science.

segments.title: Lake Placid Conferences and naming the field
segments.summary: The family unit was seen as the basic building block of improvement; the Lake Placid Conferences led to the name home economics over alternatives, and the American Home Economics Association was founded in 1908. The Smith-Hughes Act of 1917 funded vocational education.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief sponsor/ad break before returning to the history.

segments.title: Bureau of Home Economics and radio shows
segments.summary: The USDA created the Bureau of Home Economics in the 1920s, working on nutrition, meal planning, fabric testing, military food, and school lunches; radio programs such as Housekeeper's Chat and Betty Crocker Cooking School of the Air spread the field.

segments.title: Poverty line, astronaut food, and food company recipes
segments.summary: Molly Orshansky's work at the Bureau produced the federal poverty line; Bee Finkelstein helped create food for Mercury astronauts; home economists at companies like Campbell's, General Mills, and Kellogg's created label recipes, rice krispy treats, and the Chex Mix contest recipe.

segments.title: Heyday of school home ec and baby simulation
segments.summary: Describes school home ec kitchens and the egg baby and flour sack projects, which were reportedly once borrowed from orphanages, plus the Baby Think It Over simulator in the nineties; by 1959 about half of American girls took home ec.
topics: teen pregnancy prevention in home ec

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief ad break.

segments.title: Decline of home ec
segments.summary: Home ec declined from the early 1960s due to standardized testing and No Child Left Behind, the 1963 Vocational Education Act reducing funding, Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique, and a 1980s push toward STEM and vocational education under Reagan-era policy.

segments.title: Shop class and industrial arts
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh compare shop class, industrial arts, and autoshop.

segments.title: Family and Consumer Sciences rebrand and enrollment
segments.summary: Home ec was rebranded Family and Consumer Sciences in the 1990s with career focus; a 2013 report found about 3.5 million high school students took the classes in 2011-2012, a 40 percent drop from the 2000s, with 65 percent girls, and teacher shortages persist.

segments.title: Life skills, financial literacy, and obesity debate
segments.summary: Declining financial literacy and cooking skills are discussed, with some arguing they contribute to obesity and reliance on takeout; a 2024 World Economic Forum study is cited.

segments.title: Chores and parenting
segments.summary: A 2014 Braun Research study found 82 percent of parents did chores as children but only 28 percent have children doing chores; Chuck reflects on his own parenting.

segments.title: Debt, YouTube tutorials, and limits of nostalgia
segments.summary: Credit card debt and the convenience economy are discussed, along with YouTube as a way to learn skills; the hosts caution against nostalgia and note the debate about vocational education and trades, citing Nvidia's CEO on plumbers and electricians.

segments.title: Listener mail: Santa Claus Adam on the Rockettes
segments.summary: A listener email from Santa Claus Adam responds to the Rockettes select episode, describing the troupe and inviting the hosts to a show; Josh and Chuck mention a listener's birthday.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to share home ec experiences and give the email address, then sign off.
